binders: Inherited setting: x and t are real spatial and temporal variables, and q : R × R → R^m is the vector-valued unknown; m counts its components [raw PDF page 23, printed page 1, equation (1.1) and following paragraph].

The flux f acts on the state q, and f′(q) is its m × m flux Jacobian; a flux between real m-dimensional state spaces is inherited from the system's dimensions, although no state-domain set is specified [raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, equations (1.8)–(1.9); raw PDF page 23, printed page 1, definition of q and A].

At a state where the criterion is applied, there must exist m corresponding linearly independent eigenvectors with real eigenvalues. Indexing these pairs by i = 1, …, m is analyst notation for the source's 'set of m' [raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, opening hyperbolicity criterion and sentence after equation (1.9)].
hypotheses: The equation under discussion is the one-dimensional homogeneous conservation law q_t + (f(q))_x = 0, written in quasilinear form q_t + f′(q)q_x = 0 [raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, equations (1.8)–(1.9)].

The flux Jacobian f′(q) has real eigenvalues and m linearly independent corresponding eigenvectors, with the real-space interpretation supported by the stated decomposition of every vector in R^m [raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, opening paragraph and sentence after equation (1.9)].

Existence of the derivatives and applicability of the chain rule are implicit in the displayed quasilinear rewriting; no precise differentiability class is stated there [raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, 'Rewriting this in the quasilinear form' and equation (1.9)].
conclusions: The conservation-law equation is hyperbolic if its flux Jacobian satisfies the preceding real-eigenvalue and complete-independent-eigenvector criterion for A [raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, sentence immediately after equation (1.9)].
definitions_and_conventions: Subscripts t and x denote partial derivatives with respect to time and space [raw PDF page 23, printed page 1, paragraph following equation (1.1)].
f(q) is the flux function, while f′(q) denotes its Jacobian matrix with respect to the vector state q [raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, text surrounding equations (1.8)–(1.9)].

The referenced hyperbolicity condition includes a full eigenvector basis, not merely real eigenvalues: the source explicitly requires m independent eigenvectors and states that every vector in R^m has a unique expansion in them [raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, opening paragraph].
The constant linear system fits the conservation-law form through f(q) = Aq [raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, final sentence continued on raw PDF page 26, printed page 4].
implicit_context: The selected passage concerns first-order systems in one spatial dimension; the source explicitly restricts the book's discussion to first-order hyperbolic systems [raw PDF page 23, printed page 1, introduction to equation (1.1); raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, paragraph following equation (1.7)].

The pointwise spectral criterion is inherited from a constant real matrix, but f′(q) may vary with q because nonlinear fluxes are allowed [raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, equation (1.9); raw PDF page 26, printed page 4, opening paragraph].

The differential and quasilinear expressions belong to a smooth setting. The source separately warns that conservation-law solutions can be discontinuous and qualifies derivation of the differential form from the integral form by sufficient smoothness [raw PDF page 26, printed page 4, Section 1.1.2, opening paragraph].

details: Real eigenvalues and m independent corresponding eigenvectors are jointly required; reality of the eigenvalues alone is insufficient to express the stated criterion [raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, opening paragraph].
The source's unique decomposition of vectors in R^m identifies a real eigenvector basis as the intended meaning [raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, sentence immediately following the criterion].

The criterion imposes independence of eigenvectors without imposing pairwise distinct eigenvalues. Repeated eigenvalues are therefore not excluded when a full eigenvector basis exists; this is an inference from the exact listed conditions [raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, opening hyperbolicity criterion].
The matrix tested is f′(q), evaluated at the state q, rather than the flux value f(q) [raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, equation (1.9) and following sentence].
No state-independent choice of eigenvectors or eigenvalues, nor any regularity of such choices across states, is stated [raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, sentence after equation (1.9)].

The selected sentence supplies a hyperbolicity criterion. It does not state an existence, uniqueness, or regularity theorem for solutions [raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, sentence after equation (1.9)].

The wording 'suggests' connects the quasilinear rewriting to the criterion; the preceding constant-coefficient paragraph presents the referenced criterion as the meaning of hyperbolicity [raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, opening paragraph and text after equation (1.9)].

contract_plain_english: For the one-dimensional conservation law q_t + (f(q))_x = 0, the quasilinear form is q_t + f′(q)q_x = 0. The source says the equation is hyperbolic if the flux Jacobian satisfies the earlier condition for a constant real coefficient matrix: real eigenvalues together with m corresponding linearly independent eigenvectors forming a basis of R^m [raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, opening paragraph and equations (1.8)–(1.9) with the following sentence; real-state setting on raw PDF page 23, printed page 1]. The passage does not require distinct eigenvalues, specify the state domain over which the condition must hold, or prescribe a precise differentiability class. Its differential interpretation carries smoothness qualifications acknowledged in the discussion of discontinuous solutions [raw PDF page 26, printed page 4, Section 1.1.2].
